messages.subject: Min/Max Shapes from allometry - procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am enjoying the new geomorph functionality but cannot find out how to get the min and max shapes from the procD.lm() function in order to plot these with plotRefToTarget().
These shapes used to be stored in the output of the model as something like model1$shapes$min...

Specirfically, this is my code:

femur_gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(femGP, SVL = femMetaOrder$SVLmm, habitat=femMetaOrder$habitat, geoName = femMetaOrder$geoName, phyName = femMetaOrder$Phylogeny.name, genSpecies = femMetaOrder$Genspecies)
fit.size.fem <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize), data = femur_gdf)
femSizePlot <- plot(fit.size.fem, type="regression", reg.type = "RegScore", predictor = log(femur_gdf$Csize), shapes = TRUE)

and I would like to make deformed meshes representing the min and max of the allometry with something like

avgFem <- mshape(femur_gdf$coords)
plotRefToTarget(avgFem, fit.size.fem$shapes$max1)

but I cannot find the shapes and max formats

Thanks very much,

Bob Cieri

messages.subject: upsidown vectors
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm struggling with two species of my dataset which seems to have some upside down vector . When I predict the shapes (shape.predictor) for the smallest and largest specimen from the regression scores, I get a perfect adult shape for minimum values, and a neonate shape for maximum values. It's weird that it just happens with two species, and the codes are almost identical for all.

I did something like this for the six species I have analyzed (below).

Could someone tell me why it is happening?

Thanks in advance.

All the best,

Gui

Code (starting from a GPA alignment):

coords.species <- coords.subset(coords.gpa$coords, group = species)

#Lagenorhynchus
coords.gpa.Lalb <- gpagen(coords.species$Lagenorhynchus_albirostris)

fit.Lag <- procD.lm(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords ~ log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize), data=coords.gpa.Lalb, iter=0, print.progress = FALSE)

M.Lalb <- mshape(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords)

allom.plot.Lalb <- plot(fit.Lag,
                   type = "regression",
                   predictor = log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize),
                   reg.type ="RegScore")
preds.Lalb <- shape.predictor(fit.Lag$GM$fitted, x= allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore, Intercept =FALSE, predmin = min(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore), predmax = max(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore))

plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmin, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")
plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmax, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")

--

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] upsidown vectors
messages.body_plain:
This is just a guess without more evidence but min or max of regression scores does not have to correspond directly to min and max size.  It is possible to have negative scores correspond to large individuals and positive scores correspond to small individuals.  The scores in ordinations are projections on centered vectors, but the vector is arbitrarily orientated with regard to what is negative and positive (i.e., spin the vector 180 degrees and it is the same, but scores would flip from negative to positive and vice versa).

If this makes you uncomfortable you can multiply the scores by -1 before using shape predictor.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Gui,

this is not a matter of your idea being wrong. If I may give an equivalence to what Mike said, think about PCA vectors: they have no directionality, their polarity is random. In the same way, whether the regression scores are negatively or positively correlated with CS is aleatory. They ARE expressing changes in shape with respect to changes in size (at least, they are one way of doing so) but they are not bound to express changes with INCREASING size. So, to answer your question, you can use this approach to visualize shape changes throughout growth, but MATHEMATICALLY you need to make sure you are fixing the polarity of these changes from small to large organisms. To complicate things further, because you are running analyses for each species separately, the regression score vectors you are calculating are not bound to behave the same way across species, the same way the polarity of PC axes would not necessarily be the same (even if their composition were, but that´s a different issue).

Does this make sense?

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
And as a complement to my own message, on better thought, if you are interesting in visualizing the FULL set of shape changes related to size variation (allometry), you might be better off using shape.predictor on the allometry lm itself, instead of the reduced-dimension plot of regression scores. Regression scores are useful for visualizing how shape (multivariate) changes with size, mainly in the context of comparing across groups. But if your interest is on the deformations related to growth, I think looking at the full shape space related to size is a better approach.

Antigoni

In the same way, whether the regression scores are negatively or positively correlated with CS is aleatory. They ARE expressing changes in shape with respect to changes in size (at least, they are one way of doing so) but they are not bound to express changes with INCREASING size. So, to answer your question, you can use this approach to visualize shape changes throughout growth, but MATHEMATICALLY you need to make sure you are fixing the polarity of these changes from small to large organisms. To complicate things further, because you are running analyses for each species separately, the regression score vectors you are calculating are not bound to behave the same way across species, the same way the polarity of PC axes would not necessarily be the same (even if their composition were, but that´s a different issue).

I have never done anything using bilat.symmetry function and I wonder if someone could help me on how to format the file for "land.pairs" if I have 115 individuals with 14 fixed landmarks each and og those landmarks all are paired.
Thanks for your help

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am using bilat.symmetry to understand fluctuating asymmetry in a fruit fly population.

While reading through help files, I have come to understand that bilat.symmetry functions with both superimposed landmarks or raw landmark coordinates. This gave me an impression that bilat.symmetry performs superimposition in case the raw data have not been superimposed already.

However, by using both raw and superimposed coordinates in bilat.symmetry, I got different results if I just use 'coords' from gpagen. Therefore, here are the queries:

1. What are the conditions under which we should use superimposed/raw landmarks in bilat.symmmetry?
2. How is bilat.symmetry performing size anova when using 'coords' from gpagen? Isn't all configuration scaled to unit centroid size in gpagen?
3. What is difference between the results from the terms 'procD.lm.shape' and 'shape anova' after bilat.symmetry analysis?

Additional query:
4. How can I obtain DA component of each group of a population instead of a grand mean that bilat.symmetry computes by default?

Thank you in advance.

Regards
Rochishnu

Reordering coordinates can be accomplished using the match function. If you have two datasets of landmarks, lms_1 and lms_2, it could look like this:
lms_2_reordered <- lms_2[,,match(dimnames(lms_1)[[3]], dimnames(lms_2)[[3]])]

Your inputs would then be lms_1 and lms_2_reordered.

Best,
Erica Baken

Hi Geomorph folks,

I was reading a morphometrics paper this morning (Stayton et al. 2018, Evolution) and caught an interesting analysis that I would like to try out with my data.

Stayton et al. were interested in comparing morphological disparity between two groups of turtles, aquatic and terrestrial. Terrestriality has apparently evolved multiple times from aquatic ancestors. Thus, the (paraphyletic) terrestrial group might be expected to show higher disparity simply due to their distribution on the tree.

To account for the distribution of terrestrial taxa, Stayton et al. 1) calculated the ratio of aquatic to terrestrial disparity with the real data, 2) simulated shape evolution 999 times on the tree assuming a Brownian motion model of evolution 3) calculated the disparity of each simulated dataset 4) and then compared the distribution of disparities for the simulated data to the disparity of the real data.

I think it would be possible to re-use code from the compare.evol.rates function to do this with morphol.disparity, as compare.evol.rates seems to use a similar simulation procedure (when the method of simulation is chosen),  but I am having trouble interpreting the processing behind the compare.evol.rates function on the github.

Thus, my question is - how can I combine code snippets from the two functions (compare.evol.rates and morphol.disparity) to perform the analysis above?

Thank you,
Tony

messages.subject_clean: What is the difference between two formulae for morphol.disparity
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to ask what is the difference between the following two lines of code below:

morphol.disparity(coords ~ 1, groups= ~ species*site,
data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

morphol.disparity(coords ~ species*site, groups= ~species*site,
data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

These two formula differ only by the specifications on the right side of the formula. I would like to ask how should they be interpreted.

Best regards,
Lv

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] What is the difference between two formulae for morphol.disparity
messages.body_plain:
Lv,

The former analyses residuals from a model that estimates only an overall mean; the latter analyses residuals from a model that estimates species:site means.  The former will have larger residuals (in terms of distance from estimates) than the latter.  An analysis performed for the former will will ask the question, “Do any species:site groups diverge more from the overall mean than others?”  An analysis on the latter will ask, “Do species:site groups differ in the spread of values around their means.

Hope that helps!

Mike

Best, Karen
